cues.text: An Arian Kingdom
For over a century, the Visigothic kingdom of Spain had been ruled by a warrior aristocracy professing Arian Christianity .
They held that the Son of God was not fully equal to the Father.

This doctrinal divide separated the ruling Visigothic minority from the Catholic Hispano-Roman population they governed, and had periodically produced real persecution of Catholic bishops and clergy under earlier Arian kings.
A King's Conversion
King Reccared I had succeeded to the Visigothic throne in 586 and converted to Catholic orthodoxy within a year of taking power.
He was guided partly by the theological arguments of St. Leander , Bishop of Seville, and by his conviction that the kingdom's religious division had become an obstacle to its unity and stability.
In May 589, Reccared summoned a great council at Toledo , appearing before the assembled bishops in person to renounce Arianism publicly and to formally profess the Nicene faith.
A Kingdom Received Into Unity
At Reccared's urging, a substantial number of the kingdom's Arian bishops and nobles renounced their Arianism alongside their king in the same session.

They received formal reconciliation to the Catholic Church in a single dramatic and unusually rapid act of collective conversion—an outcome few earlier instances of religious division in the post-Roman West had achieved so swiftly or so completely.
This permanently ended Arianism as a significant force in Visigothic Spain.
The Filioque Question

Third Toledo is also frequently cited as containing among the earliest attestations of the word filioque — "and the Son" — inserted into the Latin recitation of the Nicene Creed's description of the Holy Spirit's procession.
In its original Spanish context, this small addition was intended to reinforce the Trinity's full equality against lingering Arian sympathies.
Whether this phrase stood in the council's own original acts or entered the transmitted text only through later manuscript revision remains genuinely debated among historians.

What is not in dispute is that the wording, wherever it first appeared in Spain, would become, many centuries later, one of the most consequential and persistent points of theological division between the Latin West and the Christian East.
Legacy
Third Toledo swiftly and thoroughly unified Visigothic Spain around Catholic orthodoxy, shaping the Spanish kingdom’s entire subsequent religious character.
It produced further Toledan councils over the following century, which developed some of the early medieval West’s most sophisticated ecclesiastical and legal institutions.
These included the seminary reforms Isidore of Seville would champion at the Fourth Council of Toledo a generation later.
Few regional councils have left so lasting and so contested a mark on the wider history of Christian doctrine as this one.
Within a single royal lifetime, it achieved a religious unification that many older and larger kingdoms of the early medieval West never fully secured at all.
